questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: explain the advantage of the polar form for multiplication
questions.stem: Explain why multiplying two complex numbers is easier in polar form than in rectangular form.

answer.exemplar: In polar form a complex number is a modulus and an angle, and the angle-addition identities for sine and cosine say that multiplying the two rectangular expansions produces only one surviving real term and one surviving imaginary term. Concretely, multiplying 3(cos α + i sin α) by 4(cos β + i sin β) gives 12(cos(α + β) + i sin(α + β)), so the whole computation reduces to multiplying 3 by 4 and adding α to β. In rectangular form the same product requires four separate multiplications and two additions before any collection of terms, because (a + bi)(c + di) = (ac − bd) + (ad + bc)i, and a sign lost in that collection gives a wrong answer with no warning. The polar rule also explains De Moivre's theorem immediately, since raising a number to the nth power multiplies the modulus by itself n times and the angle by n.

questions.explanation: A model answer must connect the angle-addition identities to the two rules for moduli and angles, since that identity is the whole reason the polar form simplifies multiplication.
questions.hint: Compare how many separate products each of the two forms needs.

Converting both numbers to rectangular form and multiplying confirms the direction: 3(cos(π/3) + i sin(π/3)) = 1.5 + 2.598i and 4(cos(-π/6) + i sin(-π/6)) = 3.464 - 2i, whose product has a positive real part and a positive imaginary part of the same size.

Multiplying that back by the divisor, 3i · 2(cos(π/3) + i sin(π/3)), recovers the original dividend, which confirms both the modulus and the angle.

a² − b², since the two squares are subtracted

Expanding directly gives 9 - 12i + 12i - 16i² = 9 + 16 = 25, since the imaginary parts cancel and -16i² becomes 16. The value -7 is what subtracting the squares would give, which is the trap for anyone who applies the difference-of-squares pattern to a plus.

questions.learningObjective: identify when a real quadratic has no real solutions
questions.stem: The equation x² + 2x + 5 = 0 has real coefficients. What is true of its solutions?

it has two real solutions, because a quadratic always has two roots
options.misconception: assumes the fundamental theorem guarantees real roots

options.misconception: blames the sign of the leading coefficient rather than the discriminant

The leading coefficient plays no part in that test; the 20 comes from 4ac, not from the sign of a. The repeated-root case would require a discriminant of zero, which is a different condition from being negative.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: interpret the discriminant of a real quadratic geometrically
questions.stem: Explain what a negative discriminant tells you about a quadratic equation with real coefficients.

answer.exemplar: The discriminant b² − 4ac of ax² + bx + c = 0 measures how far the parabola y = ax² + bx + c reaches towards the x-axis, and its sign settles the question of real roots at once. If the discriminant is negative then the vertex of the parabola lies on the opposite side of the axis from the tails, so the curve never touches the axis and the equation has no real solutions. For x² + 2x + 5 the discriminant is 4 − 20 = -16, and completing the square confirms it independently: the equation becomes (x + 1)² + 4 = 0, which asks for (x + 1)² = -4 and so has no real answer. That the two complex roots 1 + 2i and 1 - 2i come out as exact conjugates is a consequence of the coefficients being real, since a real quadratic cannot have one non-real root without its conjugate.

questions.explanation: A model answer must link the sign of the discriminant to the position of the parabola's vertex, since either the algebraic or the geometric route alone leaves the connection unstated.
questions.hint: Compare the vertex of the parabola with the x-axis, then confirm by completing the square.

options.misconception: assumes scalar commutativity extends to matrices

options.text: AB and BA are equal whenever A and B are both invertible matrices
options.misconception: believes invertibility removes the order sensitivity of a product

options.text: AB and BA are always unequal, so their product can never be computed
options.misconception: turns the possibility of a difference into a certainty

never, because the product of two nonzero quantities is never zero

This can happen with both factors nonzero, as with A having rows (1, -1) and (2, -2) multiplied by B having rows (1, 1) and (1, 1), whose product is entirely zero. That is the entry in row i, column j of B^T A^T, so the two agree entry by entry. The reversal is essential, since A^T B^T is a different matrix in general.

The second term is positive because the entries −1 and 2 have opposite signs, and that sign is the part most often lost. The value 13 comes from treating the determinant as 15 − 2, which ignores the minus sign carried by the -1.

gets the first two cofactor terms right and slips on the last sign
adds all three terms as though the cofactors were all positive

options.misconception: ignores the rows that are actually being counted

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: correct an inverse that omits the division by the determinant
questions.stem: A student claims the inverse of the 2x2 matrix A with rows (1, 2) and (3, 4) is the matrix with rows (2, -1) and (-3, 1), saying this follows from the formula for the inverse. Multiplying gives rows (-4, 1) and (-6, 1). What is wrong?

options.text: the adjugate must be divided by the determinant, which is -2, giving rows (-2, 1) and (3/2, -1/2)
the adjugate must be multiplied by the determinant, which here is -2
options.misconception: reverses the operation that the inverse formula performs

options.text: the adjugate must be transposed, since transposing reverses the sign of a determinant
options.misconception: invents a transposition step that the formula does not contain

options.text: the product shown is correct, and the identity matrix has been misremembered
options.misconception: accepts a product that is plainly not the identity

questions.explanation: The inverse of a 2x2 matrix is the adjugate divided by the determinant, and the determinant here is 1(4) - 2(3) = -2. The adjugate is the matrix the student wrote, with rows (4, -2) and (-3, 1), and dividing each entry by -2 gives rows (-2, 1) and (3/2, -1/2). Multiplying by that matrix does give the identity, which is the check the student skipped: the product they reported has entries -4 and -6 on the diagonal, so no such inverse could exist.
questions.hint: Check the determinant and whether it divides the adjugate entry by entry.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: correct a complex square computed by squaring the terms separately
questions.stem: A student claims that (1 + i)² = 1 + i² = 0, and uses this to conclude that the square of 1 + i is the real number 0. What is the correct value?

options.text: 2i, because the square expands to 1 + 2i + i² and the i² term contributes -1
0, since 1 and the square of i cancel exactly as they were written
options.misconception: applies the squaring rule to the terms instead of to the whole expression

options.text: 2, because the imaginary parts vanish whenever a number is squared
options.misconception: assumes the imaginary part disappears under squaring

options.text: -2i, because the cross term 2i is subtracted rather than added
options.misconception: reverses the sign of the cross term from the binomial expansion

questions.explanation: Squaring a binomial of complex numbers still follows the ordinary rule: (1 + i)² = 1 + 2i + i² = 1 + 2i - 1 = 2i. The cross term 2i is the part the student dropped, and it is the only survivor, since 1 + i² happens to cancel. Squaring a complex number does not remove its imaginary part, as the value 2 assumes, and the sign of the cross term is fixed by the expansion rather than chosen.
questions.hint: Expand the square as a binomial before substituting i² = -1.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: correct the claimed real roots of an equation with no real roots
questions.practice: catching a sign error in solving
questions.stem: A student says the equation x² + 4 = 0 has the two solutions x = 2 and x = -2. What is correct?

options.text: there are no real solutions, since the equation asks for x squared to equal -4
the two solutions are 2 and -2, since squaring either one gives 4
options.misconception: solves x squared equals 4 rather than x squared equals -4

options.text: the only real solution is 0, since 0 squared leaves the 4 on the right
options.misconception: treats zero as a solution to every equation of this form

options.text: the solutions are 2i and -2i, which are real because twice i is a number
options.misconception: mistakes the complex solutions for real ones

questions.explanation: Rearranging gives x² = -4, and no real number has a negative square, so the equation has no real solutions at all. Its two complex solutions are 2i and -2i, obtained from sqrt(-4), and neither is real. The student's pair 2 and -2 solves x² = 4, which is the equation that results if the 4 is moved to the right-hand side instead of being negated, and the fourth option is the trap that treats a complex number as a real one.
questions.hint: Rearrange the equation and ask whether a real square can be negative.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: justify why the identity matrix leaves a matrix unchanged
questions.stem: Explain why multiplying a square matrix A on either side by the identity matrix of the same size leaves A unchanged.

answer.exemplar: The entry in row i, column j of the identity matrix I is 1 when i = j and 0 at every other position, and each entry of a product is a dot product of a row of the first matrix with a column of the second. For the product IA, row i of I is all zeros except for a single 1 in column i, so its dot product with column j of A is that 1 times the entry of A in row i, column j, with every other term vanishing because it carries a factor of 0. Every entry of the product is thus the matching entry of A, and the same argument for AI works with the roles swapped, since column j of I is all zeros except for a 1 in row j, which picks out row j of A. The argument also shows why the identity is the only matrix with this property: any other arrangement of 1s would either select a different entry or combine several, and a scalar multiple other than 1 would rescale the whole matrix.

questions.explanation: A model answer must work through one general entry of the product rather than asserting the result, since the entrywise argument is what the property rests on.
questions.hint: Look at what a row of the identity contains, then take its dot product with a column of A.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: justify the existence of the trivial solution to a homogeneous system
questions.stem: Explain why a homogeneous system of linear equations always has the trivial solution.

answer.exemplar: A homogeneous system has zero on every right-hand side, so it takes the form Ax = 0 with 0 the zero column vector. Substituting x = 0 gives A0 = 0, because every entry of that product is the dot product of a row of A with the zero vector, and such a dot product is zero whatever the row contains. Nothing in this argument depends on the size or shape of A, on whether it is invertible, or on the number of unknowns, so the trivial solution exists for every homogeneous system over every field. The genuinely interesting question is when it is the only solution: if A is invertible, multiplying Ax = 0 by A inverse on the left forces x = 0, whereas if A is singular there is a nonzero vector in its null space, and that vector together with all its real multiples solves the system, giving infinitely many solutions. The equations 2x - 4y = 0 and x - 2y = 0 show the second case, since the second equation is half the first.

questions.explanation: A model answer must note that the argument works whether or not the coefficient matrix is invertible, since that is what makes the statement hold in every case.
questions.hint: Substitute the zero vector and check what the matrix does to it.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: carry out a row operation on an augmented matrix
questions.stem: The system x + y = 5 and x - y = 1 is written as the augmented matrix with rows (1, 1, 5) and (1, -1, 1). After carrying out the row operation R2 minus R1, what is the resulting matrix?

options.misconception: loses the negative sign on the two entries produced by the subtraction
halves the new row before reporting it
adds the two rows, which never removes the leading entry

questions.explanation: Subtracting entry by entry gives (1, -1, 1) - (1, 1, 5) = (0, -2, -4), so the second row becomes (0, -2, -4) while the first is untouched. The leading 1 has been eliminated from row 2, which is the point of the operation, and the result is in row-echelon form. Dividing the new row by 2, as the third option does, would change the pivot to 1 but is a separate operation and would scale the equation, giving y = 2 either way.
questions.hint: Subtract the whole first row from the second, entry by entry.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: apply Cramer's rule to a two by two system
questions.stem: Solve 2x + y = 7 and x + y = 5 by Cramer's rule. First compute the determinant D of the coefficient matrix, then compute the determinant D_x formed by replacing its first column with the right-hand side, and report the quotient D_x divided by D.

options.misconception: reports the determinant of the coefficient matrix instead of the quotient
reports the first right-hand side instead of the computed determinant
reports the second right-hand side instead of the computed determinant

questions.explanation: The coefficient matrix is [[2, 1], [1, 1]], so D = 2(1) - 1(1) = 1. Replacing the first column with the right-hand side gives D_x = 7(1) - 1(5) = 2, and the quotient D_x/D = 2/1 = 2, so x = 2. Substituting back, 2(2) + 3 = 7 and 2 + 3 = 5, confirming the value. The determinant D = 1 here is unusually simple, which makes it easy to report by mistake instead of the quotient.
questions.hint: Compute both determinants, keeping the column replacement straight, then divide.
